guides.title: Long and short technical invalidation distances use opposite price directions
guides.concept: A hypothetical long plan measures stop distance below entry; a hypothetical short plan measures a protective buy-stop reference above entry, using positive price units.
guides.procedure: Identify side, entry reference and technical invalidation before absolute-distance arithmetic. Reject a zero or reversed intended stop placement rather than pretending to size a valid plan.

guides.concept: A hypothetical risk-budget quotient is a theoretical upper bound on position shares, not an execution authorization or guarantee of capped loss.
guides.procedure: For a strictly positive planned per-share distance and nonnegative risk budget, compute floor(budget/distance) and separately check cash, buying power, liquidity and concentration.
guides.workedCase: FICTIONAL: $75 hypothetical risk budget divided by $0.40 technical distance gives floor(187.5)=187 shares, before liquidity and gap risk.

guides.title: Stress-loss scenarios must not assume a stop fills at its trigger
guides.concept: Stress-loss analysis calculates illustrative losses at adverse fill references to expose the difference between planned technical invalidation and execution reality.
guides.procedure: For a hypothetical long position, compare quantity×(entry−planned stop) with quantity×(entry−adverse fill), labeling both as conditional examples.
guides.workedCase: FICTIONAL: 100 shares purchased at $10 have a planned sell stop trigger $9.80 ($20 technical distance), while a hypothetical post-gap fill at $9.20 loses $80 before fees.
guides.limit: Actual fills, halts, liquidity and market gaps can differ greatly, and no finite example establishes a maximum possible loss.

guides.concept: A hypothetical target reward must account for price movement and explicitly modeled execution costs; favorable prices alone do not establish net gains.
guides.procedure: State entry, planned target, per-share expected round-trip friction and quantity; compute (target−entry−cost) for a long illustrative scenario.

guides.title: Cost-adjusted reward/risk depends on both cost and adverse exit modeling
guides.concept: A cost-adjusted planned reward-to-risk ratio uses consistent per-share net reward and per-share modeled adverse loss, each under stated execution assumptions.
guides.procedure: Compute net reward=(target−entry−target-side cost) and modeled loss=(entry−stop reference+stop-side cost); divide only by a positive loss denominator.

guides.limit: The ratio is conditional planning arithmetic and cannot replace a probability estimate or reflect unmodeled gap losses.
